questions.q: What does it mean for a setup script to be idempotent?
options: It runs faster each time it's executed
It produces the same end state whether it's run once or many times
It only works on one server at a time
It deletes itself after running once
questions.explain: An idempotent script checks the current state before changing anything, so rerunning it doesn't fail or duplicate work -- the end result is identical no matter how many times it runs.

questions.q: Why does the script run `id -u "$USERNAME" &>/dev/null` before calling `useradd`?
options: To print the user's password to the terminal
To check whether the user already exists, so the script doesn't fail by trying to create a duplicate account
Because useradd requires id -u to be run first by law
To measure how long the script has been running
questions.explain: id -u exits with a non-zero status if the user doesn't exist. Checking that first lets the script skip creation on a rerun instead of failing on a duplicate-user error.

questions.q: Why does the script check with `grep -qF` before appending a key to authorized_keys, instead of always appending?
options: grep is required by sshd before any key can be used
To avoid appending the same public key twice if the script runs again
Appending without grep first would corrupt the file format
grep -qF encrypts the key before writing it
questions.explain: Always appending would duplicate the key every time the script reruns. Checking with grep -qF first keeps authorized_keys clean no matter how many times setup runs.

questions.q: Why do chmod 700 and chmod 600 run unconditionally on every execution, rather than only when the .ssh directory is first created?
options: Because chmod can only be run once per server
Running them every time is harmless when permissions are already correct, and self-heals them if something changed the permissions since the last run
They have to run before useradd or the script crashes
chmod is only needed for the username, not the SSH directory
questions.explain: Setting permissions unconditionally is itself idempotent -- it's a no-op when they're already right, and it quietly fixes them if anything (or anyone) changed them in between runs.

questions.q: In the Python fleet-wide wrapper, what does checking `result.returncode` after each `subprocess.run()` call accomplish?
options: It prevents the SSH connection from ever timing out
It identifies which specific server's setup failed, so that failure is logged and visible instead of silently skipped
It automatically retries the failed server a second time
It has no effect since subprocess.run() always succeeds
questions.explain: A non-zero returncode means that server's run failed. Checking it per-server means one bad server gets logged and flagged, rather than the loop plowing ahead as if everything succeeded.
